title: Data Through Pictures: Pictographs, Bar Graphs and Line Graphs
seo_title: Pictographs, Bar Graphs and Line Graphs Class 5 Worksheet with Answers (Maths Mela Chapter 15)
standard_code: Class 5, Maths Mela Chapter 15: Data Through Pictures
standard_text: Data handling: collecting and representing data in tables, pictographs and bar graphs, reading line graphs, and interpreting data (summary of NCERT Maths Mela Class 5)
meta_desc: Class 5 Data Through Pictures worksheet (Maths Mela Chapter 15): tables, bar graphs, double bar graphs, line graphs and conclusions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Read the title, axes and scale first.
key_sub: Line graphs show change over time.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • A bar graph compares amounts; a double bar graph compares two sets side by side.
  • A line graph shows how something changes over time.

Examples

Example

The line rises from 20 to 35 between May and June.

35 − 20

Answer: It rose by 15

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Reading between grid lines wronglyWork out what each grid step is worth.
Mixing up the two barsCheck the key for each colour.

faq.q: When is a line graph used?
faq.a: To show how something changes over time, like temperature through a day.

faq.q: What is a double bar graph?
faq.a: A bar graph comparing two groups for each category.

items.q: How many students in 5B have a packed lunch?
items.e: Find the Packed lunch row, then go across to the 5B column: 9. (11 is 5A.)

items.q: How many students in 5A have a school dinner?
items.e: School dinner row, 5A column: 14.

items.q: How many students are in 5A?
items.e: The Total row at the bottom gives each class. 5A: 14 + 11 + 3 = 28.

items.q: How many more students have a school dinner than a packed lunch?
items.e: Use the Total column. School dinner: 31. Packed lunch: 20. 31 − 20 = 11. (Using only one class gives 3 or 8.)

items.q: How many students are in Class 5 altogether?
items.e: The bottom right cell is the total of everything: 28 + 30 = 58 students.

items.q: What time does the swimming pool close on Saturday?
items.e: Find the Saturday row, then go across to the Closes column: 17:30 (5:30 pm).

items.q: How long is the pool open on Sunday?
items.e: 09:30 to 15:30 is 6 hours. 15:30 to 16:00 is 30 minutes. So the pool is open 6 hours 30 minutes. (1,600 − 930 = 670 treats an hour as 100 minutes.)

items.q: On which day is the pool open for the longest time?
items.e: Work out each day: Monday 13 hours 30 minutes, Wednesday 15 hours, Saturday 9 hours 30 minutes, Sunday 6 hours 30 minutes. Wednesday is the longest. (Monday opens just as early, but closes earlier.)

items.q: How many adult tickets were sold on Friday?
items.e: The adult row adds up to 183. Thursday is 86. 183 − 86 = 97 tickets. Check: 86 + 97 = 183.

items.q: How many child tickets were sold altogether?
items.e: Add along the Child row: 124 + 158 = 282. Remember to exchange: 4 + 8 = 12 ones.

items.q: What number is missing from the table?
items.e: The bottom right cell is the total of all tickets. Add the Total column: 183 + 282 = 465. Check with the Total row: 210 + 255 = 465.

items.q: On which day were more child tickets sold, and how many more?
items.e: Child row: Thursday 124, Friday 158. Friday is more: 158 − 124 = 34.

items.q: How many boys cannot swim 25 m?
items.e: There are 45 boys. 38 of them can swim. 45 − 38 = 7 boys cannot.

items.q: How many students can swim 25 m?
items.e: Add down the Can column: 38 + 41 = 79. (92 is everyone in Class 5, and 13 is the Cannot column.)

items.q: The bus leaves the Bus Station at 09:15. What time does it get to the Hospital?
items.e: Find 09:15 in the Bus Station row. Go down that column (Bus 2) to the Hospital row: 09:49.

items.q: Which bus does not stop at the Library?
items.e: A dash (—) means the bus does not stop there. The dash in the Library row is in the Bus 3 column.

items.q: How long does Bus 1 take from the Bus Station to the Retail Park?
items.e: 08:45 to 09:00 is 15 minutes. 09:00 to 09:32 is 32 minutes. 15 + 32 = 47 minutes. (87 minutes uses 100 minutes in an hour.)

items.q: How long does Bus 1 take from the High Street to the Library?
items.e: High Street 08:58, Library 09:06. 08:58 to 09:06 is 8 minutes.

items.q: Arjun gets to the High Street at 09:31, just after a bus has left. How long must he wait for the next bus?
items.e: The bus at 09:28 has gone. The next bus at the High Street is at 09:58. From 09:31 to 09:58 is 27 minutes.

items.q: How long does it take to go from the High Street to the Hospital?
items.e: Use any bus that stops at both. Bus 2: High Street 09:28, Hospital 09:49. 09:28 to 09:49 is 21 minutes.

items.q: What does the legend on a double bar graph tell you?
c: The total of all the bars
items.e: The legend (or key) matches each colour to a group, such as green for Class 5A and orange for Class 5B. The source tells where the data came from.

items.q: Why does a double bar graph have two bars for each category?
items.e: Each pair has one bar for each group, side by side, so you can see at once which group has more.

items.q: How many students in Class 5A have a dog?
items.e: Class 5A is green in the legend. The green Dog bar reaches the line labelled 8. (6 is the orange Class 5B bar, 14 adds both bars, and 2 is the difference.)

items.q: How many students in Class 5B have a cat?
items.e: Class 5B is orange. The orange Cat bar ends one line above 6, so it shows 7. (5 is the green Class 5A bar, and 12 adds both bars.)

items.q: How many students in Class 5B have no pet?
items.e: Find the orange bar above “No pet”. It reaches the line labelled 6. (9 is the green Class 5A bar, 15 adds both bars, and 3 is the difference.)

items.q: Which class has more students with fish?
items.e: For Fish, the orange Class 5B bar (4) is taller than the green Class 5A bar (2).

items.q: Which answer was the most common in Class 5A?
items.e: The tallest green bar is “No pet”, with 9 students. (Dog has 8. Cat is the tallest orange bar, for Class 5B.)

items.q: How many more students in Class 5A than in Class 5B have a dog?
items.e: Dog: Class 5A has 8 and Class 5B has 6. 8 − 6 = 2 more students. (14 adds the two bars.)

items.q: Every student in Class 5A answered. How many students are in Class 5A?
items.e: Add the green bars: 8 + 5 + 2 + 9 = 24. (23 adds the orange Class 5B bars, 47 adds both classes, and 9 is only the tallest bar.)

items.q: Every student in Class 5B answered. How many students are in Class 5B?
items.e: Add the orange bars: 6 + 7 + 4 + 6 = 23. (24 adds the green Class 5A bars, and 7 is only the tallest bar.)

items.q: How many books did 5A read in October?
items.e: 5A is green. The green October bar reaches the line labelled 18. (20 is the orange 5B bar, 9 counts the grid lines as 1 each, but each line stands for 2, and 38 adds both bars.)

items.q: How many books did 5B read in November?
items.e: The orange November bar reaches the line labelled 16. (11 is the green 5A bar, 8 counts grid lines instead of reading the scale, and 27 adds both bars.)

items.q: How many books did 5A read in November?
items.e: The green November bar ends halfway between 10 and 12. Halfway between them is 11. (12 and 10 are the lines on each side, and 16 is the orange 5B bar.)

items.q: In which month did both classes read the same number of books?
items.e: In December both bars reach 16, so the two bars are the same height.

items.q: In which month did 5A read more books than 5B?
items.e: Only in September is the green 5A bar taller: 14 books for 5A and 12 for 5B.

items.q: Which bars show 5B?
c: The taller bar in each pair
items.e: The legend shows that orange is 5B. The taller bar is not always 5B: in September the green bar is taller.

items.q: In October, which class read more books, and how many more?
items.e: October: 5B (orange) read 20 and 5A (green) read 18. 20 − 18 = 2. (1 more counts the grid lines, but each line stands for 2, and 38 adds the bars.)

items.q: What is the greatest number of books one class read in one month?
items.e: The tallest bar is the orange 5B bar for October. It reaches 20. (18 is the tallest green bar, 38 adds October’s two bars, and 10 counts grid lines.)

items.q: On a double bar graph, the green bar for football is taller than the orange bar for football. What does this mean?
c: The green group chose football more
The orange group chose football more
items.e: In a pair, the taller bar shows the bigger number. It tells you nothing about the other sports.

items.q: Ishaan is asked about Class 5A (green), but she reads the orange bar. What should she do first?
c: Check the legend for the colour
items.e: The legend tells which colour is Class 5A. Find that colour in the pair, then read the scale.

items.q: On the temperature scale, what is each small square worth?
items.e: The labels go 0, 5, 10, 15, 20. There are 5 small squares between two labels. 5 ÷ 5 = 1, so each small square is 1 °C.

items.q: What was the temperature at 10:00?
items.e: Go up from 10:00 to the point, then across to the scale. It is 1 small square above 10, so 11 °C.

items.q: What was the highest temperature?
items.e: The highest point is at 14:00. It is 3 small squares above 15, so 18 °C. (20 °C is the top of the scale, not a reading.)

items.q: What was the lowest temperature?
items.e: The lowest point is at 06:00. It is 4 small squares above 0, so 4 °C. (6 is the time, 06:00, not the temperature.)

items.q: At what time was the temperature 13 °C?
items.e: Find 13 on the scale (3 small squares above 10). Go across to the line and down: 16:00.

items.q: On the distance scale, what is each small square worth?
items.e: The labels go up in 200s. There are 2 small squares between two labels, so each square is 200 ÷ 2 = 100 m.

items.q: How far from home was Meera at 10:20?
items.e: At 10:20 the point is halfway between the lines for 600 and 700, so 650 m.

items.q: The park is the furthest point from home on Meera’s walk. How far from home is the park?
items.e: The highest part of the line is at 900 m (1 small square below 1,000). (1,800 m is there and back.)

items.q: Meera stopped at the park. When was she at the park?
items.e: When Meera stops, her distance from home does not change, so the line is flat. From 10:30 to 10:40 it stays at 900 m.

items.q: At 11:00 the line is back at 0 m. What does this mean?
items.e: The graph shows the distance from home. 0 m from home means Meera is at home again. She walked to the park and back.

items.q: What is each small square on the water scale worth?
items.e: The labels go up in 1,000s. There are 2 small squares between two labels, so each square is 1,000 ÷ 2 = 500 L.

items.q: How much water was in the tank on Tuesday?
items.e: Go up from Tue to the dot. It is on the line halfway between 3,000 and 4,000, so 3,500 L.

items.q: How much water was in the tank on Friday?
items.e: Each small square is 500 L. On Friday the dot is halfway between the lines for 4,000 and 4,500. Halfway between them is 4,250 L.

items.q: On which day were there 3,750 L of water in the tank?
items.e: 3,750 L is halfway between 3,500 and 4,000. The dot halfway between those lines is above Sat, so Saturday.

items.q: What was the most water in the tank during the week?
items.e: The highest dot is on Thursday, on the line halfway between 4,000 and 5,000: 4,500 L. (5,000 L is the top of the scale, not a reading.)

items.q: What is each small square on the height scale worth?
items.e: The labels go up in 20s. There are 2 small squares between two labels, so each square is 20 ÷ 2 = 10 cm.

items.q: How tall was the sunflower in week 2?
items.e: In week 2 the dot is halfway between the lines for 30 and 40, so 35 cm. (20 cm is week 1.)

items.q: How tall was the sunflower in week 4?
items.e: In week 4 the dot is on the labelled line for 80, so 80 cm. (8 cm counts each small square as 1 cm.)

items.q: In which week did the sunflower first reach 1 metre (100 cm)?
items.e: Find 100 on the scale. The first dot on that line is in week 5. (In week 4 it was only 80 cm.)

items.q: How tall was the sunflower when it was first measured, in week 0?
items.e: Week 0 is the first dot. It is on the first small line above 0, so 10 cm. (The sunflower was already 10 cm tall, not 0 cm.)

items.q: Between which two days did the amount of water go up?
items.e: The line goes up only once: from Wednesday (3,000 L) to Thursday (4,500 L). Everywhere else it goes down.

items.q: By how much did the water go up from Wednesday to Thursday?
items.e: Thursday 4,500 L − Wednesday 3,000 L = 1,500 L. (3 is the number of small squares; each square is 500 L.)

items.q: How much water was used from Monday to Wednesday?
items.e: Monday 4,000 L, Wednesday 3,000 L. 4,000 − 3,000 = 1,000 L. (500 L is only one day.)

items.q: From Friday to Sunday the line falls by the same amount each day. How much water was used each day?
items.e: Friday 4,250 L, Saturday 3,750 L, Sunday 3,250 L. Each day it fell by 500 L. (1,000 L is the total for 2 days.)

items.q: What does the rise from Wednesday to Thursday most likely show?
c: The family used a lot of water
Rain added water to the tank
items.e: Using water makes the line go down. The line goes up, so water was added to the tank, most likely by rain.

items.q: How much mass did the puppy gain from 2 months to 8 months?
items.e: 2 months: 3 kg. 8 months: 12 kg. Gain = 12 − 3 = 9 kg. (6 is the number of months.)

items.q: Between which two ages did the puppy gain the most mass?
items.e: Find the steepest part. 3 to 4 months: 8 − 5 = 3 kg. Every other step is 2 kg or less. (At 7 and 8 months the puppy is heaviest, but it is not gaining mass.)

items.q: Between which two ages did the puppy’s mass stay the same?
items.e: A flat line shows no change. From 7 to 8 months the line stays on 12 kg.

items.q: What does the flat part of the line at the end show?
c: The puppy’s mass did not change
items.e: A flat line means the value stays the same: 12 kg at 7 months and at 8 months. The graph does not tell us anything about eating.

items.q: Between which two counts did the number of people go up the most?
items.e: 10 am to 12 pm: 225 − 125 = 100 people. 8 am to 10 am: 75. 12 pm to 2 pm: 50. The steepest rise is 10 am to 12 pm, not the part that reaches the highest point.

items.q: Between which two counts did the number of people go down the most?
items.e: 2 pm to 4 pm: 275 − 200 = 75 fewer. 4 pm to 6 pm: 200 − 75 = 125 fewer. So 4 pm to 6 pm.

items.q: How many more people were at the beach at 2 pm than at 8 am?
items.e: 2 pm: 275. 8 am: 50. How many more means subtract: 275 − 50 = 225. (9 is the number of small squares; each one is 25 people.)

items.q: Between which two weeks did the sunflower grow the most?
items.e: Find the steepest part. Week 3 to week 4: 80 − 55 = 25 cm. Week 4 to 5: 20 cm. Week 5 to 6: only 10 cm, even though week 6 is the tallest.

items.q: How much did the sunflower grow from week 4 to week 6?
items.e: Week 4: 80 cm. Week 6: 110 cm. 110 − 80 = 30 cm.

items.q: How tall was Varun’s sunflower in week 2?
items.e: Varun is the dashed line. In week 2 it is on the line for 40, so 40 cm. (35 cm is Neha’s.)

items.q: How tall was Varun’s sunflower in week 6?
items.e: Week 6, dashed line: halfway between 110 and 120, so 115 cm. (110 cm is Neha’s.)

items.q: In which week were the two sunflowers the same height?
items.e: Look for the place where the two lines meet. In week 3 both are 55 cm.

items.q: Whose sunflower was taller in week 5, and by how much?
items.e: Week 5: Neha 100 cm, Varun 85 cm. Neha’s is taller: 100 − 85 = 15 cm.

items.q: In how many of the weeks was Varun’s sunflower taller than Neha’s?
items.e: The dashed Varun line is above the solid line in weeks 0, 1, 2 and 6. In week 3 they are the same, so it does not count.

items.q: In which week was the difference between the two heights the biggest?
items.e: Find the biggest gap between the lines. Week 5: 15 cm. Week 1 and week 4: 10 cm. Week 6: 5 cm. (Week 6 has the tallest sunflower, not the biggest gap.)

items.q: Which statement is supported by the graph?
c: The family used 500 L every day
The tank was empty on Wednesday
It will rain again next Thursday
There was more water on Thursday than on Monday
items.e: Thursday: 4,500 L. Monday: 4,000 L. The water did not fall by 500 L every day (Thursday to Friday it fell 250 L). The graph cannot tell us about next week. On Wednesday there were still 3,000 L.

items.q: After Sunday the family keeps using 500 L each day, and it does not rain. How much water will be in the tank on Tuesday?
The tank can hold 5,000 L. How much more water could it hold on Thursday?
items.e: On Thursday it held 4,500 L. 5,000 − 4,500 = 500 L more would fill it.

items.q: Varun says, “My sunflower grew more than Neha’s, because it is taller in week 6.” Is he right?
items.e: Neha: 110 − 10 = 100 cm. Varun: 115 − 15 = 100 cm. They grew the same amount. Varun’s started taller, so it finished taller. (115 cm and 110 cm are heights, not growth.)

items.q: Which statement is supported by the dot plot?
c: Half the class has no pets
Students with more pets are happier
More students have 1 pet than any other number
items.e: 1 pet has the tallest stack (9 dots). Only 4 of the 24 students have no pets, which is not half. The dot plot does not tell us how happy anyone is.

items.q: Which statement is supported by the graph?
c: There are 275 people at 2 pm every Saturday
The beach was busiest at 2 pm
The beach was busiest at 6 pm
It rained at 6 pm, so people went home
items.e: The highest point is at 2 pm (275 people). The graph does not show the weather, and it is one Saturday only, so it cannot tell us about every Saturday.

items.q: The surf club wants 1 lifeguard on duty for every 50 people at the beach (or part of 50). How many lifeguards are needed at 2 pm?
items.e: At 2 pm there were 275 people. 5 lifeguards cover 5 × 50 = 250 people. 25 people are left over, so 1 more is needed: 6 lifeguards.

items.q: Dev’s puppy weighed 3 kg at 2 months. At what age did it first weigh more than 3 times as much?
items.e: 3 × 3 kg = 9 kg. At 4 months it was 8 kg, which is not more than 9 kg. At 5 months it was 10 kg, so 5 months.

items.q: Neha’s sunflower keeps growing the same amount each week as it did from week 5 to week 6. How tall will it be in week 8?
items.e: From week 5 to week 6 it grew 110 − 100 = 10 cm. Two more weeks: 110 + 10 + 10 = 130 cm.

items.q: Swimmers who swam 8 laps or more can join the relay team for the swimming carnival. How many swimmers is that?
items.e: 8 laps or more means 8 and 12 (nobody swam 9, 10 or 11). 2 + 1 = 3 swimmers.

items.q: Size M shirts come in packs of 5. How many packs must the school order so every student who needs size M gets one?
items.e: 12 students need size M. 2 packs give 10 shirts, which is not enough. 3 packs give 15 shirts, so order 3 packs.

items.q: How many families have more than 4 people?
items.e: More than 4 means 5 or 6 people: 5 + 2 = 7 families. Families with exactly 4 people do not count.

items.q: How many fewer students came by car in spring than in autumn?
items.e: Car: autumn 10, spring 4. 10 − 4 = 6 fewer. (14 adds the bars, 4 is one bar, and 3 counts grid lines.)

items.q: Which is a reasonable reason for the changes from autumn to spring?
c: The graph uses a scale of 2
Spring weather is better for biking
Fewer students are in the class
items.e: More students biked and walked in spring, and fewer came by car. Nicer spring weather is a sensible reason. The class size did not change: 34 students both times.

items.q: To compare the favourite sports of Class 5 and Class 6, Aditya asks only the players on his hockey team. What is the problem?
c: His team will likely choose hockey
items.e: Hockey players are likely to choose hockey, so the graph would not show what all students like. He should ask students from all the classes.

items.q: A graph’s scale starts at 50, not 0. The Class 5 bar shows 60 and the Class 6 bar shows 55, so the Class 5 bar looks twice as tall. Is Class 5 really twice as much?
c: Yes: its bar is twice as tall
items.e: From 50, the bars are 10 and 5 units tall, so one looks twice as tall. But 60 is not twice 55. Always read the numbers on the scale.

items.q: Each dot is one student. What is the mode of the data?
items.e: The mode is the value that appears most often: the tallest stack of dots. 9 students have 1 pet, so the mode is 1 pet. (9 is how many students, and 6 is the highest value, not the mode.)

items.q: How many students have 2 pets?
items.e: Count the dots above 2: there are 6. Each dot is one student.

items.q: How many students are in 5C?
items.e: Each dot is one student, so count all the dots: 4 + 9 + 6 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 24. (40 is the total number of pets, not students.)

items.q: How many students have no pets?
items.e: No pets is the value 0. There are 4 dots above 0.
